plain_text:
Researchers at the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research used an innovative
technique to visualize pain signals in mice's facial nerves in real time. Their findings could
help scientists develop safer ways to treat pain in the face, mouth, and jaw.
semantic_text: Researchers at the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research used an innovative technique to visualize pain signals in mice's facial nerves in real time. Their findings could help scientists develop safer ways to treat pain in the face, mouth, and jaw.

plain_text:
Pain is your body's way of telling you that something might
be wrong and is the most frequent reason people seek
medical care.
semantic_text: Pain is your body's way of telling you that something might be wrong and is the most frequent reason people seek medical care.

plain_text:
Facial and oral pain (in the face, mouth, and jaw) can be
a symptom of injury, illness, or infection. It is one of the
most common causes of pain complaints after neck, back,
and knee pain.
semantic_text: Facial and oral pain (in the face, mouth, and jaw) can be a symptom of injury, illness, or infection. It is one of the most common causes of pain complaints after neck, back, and knee pain.

plain_text:
Researchers at the National Institute of Dental and
Craniofacial Research (NIDCR) wanted to explore new
ways to treat facial pain without unwanted side effects.
Two research teams joined forces to learn how nerves in
the face send and receive information about pain. One
team studies the biology of sensations such as pain, and
the other has expertise in cell imaging.
semantic_text: Researchers at the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR) wanted to explore new ways to treat facial pain without unwanted side effects. Two research teams joined forces to learn how nerves in the face send and receive information about pain. One team studies the biology of sensations such as pain, and the other has expertise in cell imaging.

plain_text:
Ashok B. Kulkarni, Ph.D., has spent years studying a protein
called cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5). Cdk5 is involved in
pain signaling in other parts of the body, and Dr. Kulkarni
and his team wanted to understand its role in facial pain.
semantic_text: Ashok B. Kulkarni, Ph.D., has spent years studying a protein called cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5). Cdk5 is involved in pain signaling in other parts of the body, and Dr. Kulkarni and his team wanted to understand its role in facial pain.

plain_text:
To find out, they took mice and exposed parts of their
faces to different kinds of stimuli: gentle brushing, poking,
heat, and chili extract.
semantic_text: To find out, they took mice and exposed parts of their faces to different kinds of stimuli: gentle brushing, poking, heat, and chili extract.

plain_text:
Allodynia means "other pain."
It is a symptom of nerve pain.
It is linked to certain conditions
that target the nerves such as
migraine and fibromyalgia.
semantic_text: Allodynia means "other pain." It is a symptom of nerve pain. It is linked to certain conditions that target the nerves such as migraine and fibromyalgia.

plain_text:
A burn, cut, or other painful stimuli like spicy food
activates receptors on the skin's nerve endings. This
triggers an influx of calcium, which acts as a message to
the brain. The technique they used—called “fluorescence
microscopy”—allowed the research team to watch this
happen in real time as the individual cells in the mice's
facial nerves responded to each of the stimuli.
semantic_text: A burn, cut, or other painful stimuli like spicy food activates receptors on the skin's nerve endings. This triggers an influx of calcium, which acts as a message to the brain. The technique they used—called “fluorescence microscopy”—allowed the research team to watch this happen in real time as the individual cells in the mice's facial nerves responded to each of the stimuli.

plain_text:
"You see calcium go up and that [looks like] a flash
of light," explained Kenneth M. Yamada, M.D., Ph.D.,
an NIH Distinguished Investigator. Dr. Yamada, who is
Chief of the NIDCR Cell Biology Section, has expertise in
developmental biology.
